claims.text: The ball-milled Mg-Al-Ti-V-Fe-Co powder is a single-phase BCC solid solution.
The ball-milled powder has high lattice strain.
The ball-milled powder may contain oxygen contamination.
SPS at 950–1000 °C triggers decomposition of the metastable BCC solid solution into a BCC matrix and secondary Laves phases.
The secondary phase is a Ti/V-rich Laves phase such as (Mg,Al)2(Ti,V).
Nanometer-scale Laves precipitates form a continuous network at BCC grain boundaries.
Laves-phase precipitation reduces atomic-radius misfit and the elastic energy of the solid solution.
The grain-boundary precipitates impede outward Mg diffusion and suppress Mg volatility.
The grain-boundary precipitates impede inward oxygen diffusion.
The barrier mechanism promotes a dense, continuous Cr/Ti-rich oxide scale rather than porous spinels.
The proposed sintering window produces a bulk alloy exceeding 98% theoretical density.
Refined microstructure and second-phase strengthening increase hardness.
The alloy produced in the proposed window has Vickers hardness above 600 Hv.
Oxidation of the optimally sintered material follows linear kinetics.
The optimally sintered material has a significantly lower parabolic oxidation rate constant than material sintered below 800 °C or above 1000 °C.
The oxide scale is dense and adherent and lacks MgO-rich porous layers.
Sintering below 800 °C provides insufficient driving force, resulting in low density and no phase separation.
Sintering above 1000 °C causes rapid Mg evaporation and composition deviation.
Mg loss above 1000 °C disrupts the stoichiometry needed for Laves-phase formation and creates a porous, non-protective microstructure.
The mechanism fails when sintering time is too short for nucleation and growth of the barrier-forming precipitates.

contradictions.description: The stated alloy contains Mg, Al, Ti, V, Fe, and Co but no Cr, whereas the mechanism requires formation of a continuous Cr/Ti-rich oxide scale.

The outcome simultaneously specifies a linear oxidation regime and compares parabolic rate constants. Linear and parabolic kinetic laws are distinct, so the intended kinetic model is internally inconsistent.
